newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania turns NATO disappointment into future hope.
newsitem.headline: Romania turns NATO disappointment into future hope.

text.p: Romania, bowing to Washington's decision to pass it over for early admission to NATO, is wooing European friends for help to secure membership at a later date.

Reformist President Emil Constantinescu was not put off by the United States' choice to support only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as the first ex-communist states invited join the alliance at its July 8-9 summit in Madrid.

Constantinescu, who goes to Bonn for talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl on July 2, admits that his country lags behind the three favourites in economic reform. But he insists it is attractive for military and strategic reasons.
He says the best deal Romania should expect from the Madrid summit would be firm guarantees of gaining later entry into NATO.

"Romania's first-wave admission to NATO is a closed chapter now," he told reporters on Friday, returning from the Netherlands, current European Union president, where Central and East European leaders were briefed about EU enlargement prospects after the EU summit in Amsterdam last week.
Saddled with its economic lag, Romania has also struggled to remove the stigma of inter-ethnic and political violence which rocked the country in the early post-communist years.

"Nobody could really expect that a gap of seven years could be bridged in just seven months," a local political analyst said. "We may have missed NATO's first train, but at least now we're sure of getting on board at the next stop."

France, Romania's long-standing friend, has mustered support from European allies and from Canada, for Romania and Slovenia to be also considered for early membership, saying their admission would strengthen NATO's southern flank.
"If Germany adds to France's support that might lead to a reasonable compromise for Romania," said Constantinescu. Bonn has said it is open to NATO enlargement with three, four or five new members.
The first glimpse of a possible compromise solution came from Washington, after Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's visit last week to United States.
The White House has announced that Bill Clinton would travel to Bucharest on July 11, after attending NATO's 16-nation summit in Madrid.
Clinton, the first U.S. president to visit the Balkan country in 20 years, will make clear that Romania is a "leading candidate for future entry" into NATO, the White House said.

Clinton has been among Western leaders who have praised the new Romanian leadership for bringing ethnic Hungarians into the government after the centrists ended the ex-communists' seven-year grip on power in the November 1996 elections.

New treaties ending rifts over borders and minorities with neighbours Hungary and the former Soviet republic of Ukraine have also boosted Romania's hopes of eventual integration into Western political, security and economic structures.
Constantinescu has told fellow Romanians that the country, bordering the Black Sea, was now "more secure than ever."

"Never in its history has Romania been more secure of its independence and territorial integrity than now," he told a news conference on Thursday, marking his first 200 days in power since he ousted an ex-communist in last year's polls.

His predecessor, Ion Iliescu, accused the centrists of "instilling Romanians with false hopes of gaining quick admission to NATO". His leftists had also tried to steer Romania closer to Western structures before 1996.
